item.title: Thousands join Amsterdam climate march ahead of budget day
item.description:
Thousands join Amsterdam climate march ahead of budget day

September 12, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Tens of thousands of people marched through Amsterdam on Saturday to call on the government to end its reliance on fossil fuels, three days before the cabinet presents its annual budget plan.

Organisers the Klimaatcrisis Coalitie, an alliance of Greenpeace, Milieudefensie, Extinction Rebellion and around 200 other groups, said more than 40,000 people took part.

The 2.5 kilometre route ran from the Dam to Museumplein, with 43 organised blocs including a youth bloc, a tech bloc and one from trade union federation FNV.

ANP reported many placards had the word “klimaatdrammer” – the “climate nag” label prime minister Rob Jetten adopted as a badge of honour after a VVD MP used it against him in 2019.

The coalition wants the government to end fossil fuel subsidies and speed up the switch to wind and solar rather than nuclear. Spokeswoman Merel Fiets said early reports on the leaked budget were “not encouraging” and that current policy would not meet the climate targets.

Organisers said climate minister Stientje van Veldhoven was handed their demands at a press conference before the march but announced no new measures.

item.title: Cabinet to stop employers docking foreign workers’ pay for rent
item.description:
Cabinet to stop employers docking foreign workers’ pay for rent

September 11, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Employers will no longer be allowed to deduct rent from foreign workers’ minimum wage from July 2028, social affairs minister Hans Vijlbrief has told parliament.

Under current rules, employers and agencies can withhold up to 25% of the minimum wage – around €144 a week – to cover accommodation, provided the housing is certified.

The scheme is used mainly for the estimated 600,000 to 900,000 foreign workers in the Netherlands, most of them from Poland, Romania, Hungary and Ukraine, who work in meat processing, distribution centres and greenhouses.

Research by the ministry found employers regularly deduct the full 25% even when the quality of the housing does not justify it, Vijlbrief wrote in a letter to parliament on Thursday.

He said employers are using the deductions as a “business model” and told Nieuwsuur that too many people are being exploited.

Employers will still be able to provide housing, but will have to charge for it separately and at a fair price, the minister said. Ending deductions will also make it easier for inspectors to check whether workers are actually being paid minimum wage, he said.

The decision is the cabinet’s third on the issue in little over a year. Eddy van Hijum, former social affairs minister, proposed phasing out the deductions from January 2026, but his successor Mariëlle Paul of the VVD reversed that decision, arguing that workers would struggle to find housing without employer involvement.

Trade union federation FNV called the move a “perverse profit model at the expense of migrant workers”, and parliament has twice voted for the deductions to go.

Vijlbrief acknowledged that the ban will mean foreign workers will have to find their own accommodation amid the housing crisis. As a result, the ban will come with a rent protection bill, which has yet to reach parliament. Both are scheduled for July 1, 2028.

The measure is part of a wider package to tackle the exploitation of foreign workers, including a ban on temp agency staff in the meat industry, also from mid-2028. A long-delayed licensing system for staffing agencies is set to take effect in 2027.

item.title: Cabinet backs EU-wide minimum age for social media
item.description:
Cabinet backs EU-wide minimum age for social media

September 11, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The government has backed an EU-wide minimum age for social media, ahead of proposals from Brussels expected next week.

The Netherlands and Spain have sent joint proposals to the European Commission calling for a single minimum age across the bloc, with privacy-friendly age checks.

European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen is expected to outline how the bloc can can limit social media by children in her annual State of the Union speech to the European Parliament next Wednesday.

“In the physical world we do not accept that products are unsafe for children,” junior digital economy minister Willemijn Aerdts (D66) said in a statement. “The same standard must apply online.”

D66, VVD and CDA agreed in their coalition agreement to push for an enforceable European minimum age of 15. The joint paper with Spain does not name an age, but Aerdts told broadcaster NOS that 15 remains the Dutch position.

Australia became the first country in the world to bar under-16s from platforms such as Facebook and Instagram in December 2025. France’s ban on under-15s took effect this month, and the UK has announced a ban on under-16s from 2027.

The proposal faces criticism, including from privacy advocates worried about how age verification would work in practice.

Brussels unveiled an age-check app in April, but a security researcher demonstrated a way to bypass it within hours of the launch, and the commission had to issue a patch.

item.title: Feyenoord bans 47 fans over Cambuur fireworks barrage
item.description:
Feyenoord bans 47 fans over Cambuur fireworks barrage

September 11, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Feyenoord has banned 47 supporters from De Kuip stadium over the fireworks barrage that injured seven Cambuur fans during last month’s match in Leeuwarden, the club said on Friday.

The 47 have also had their away-match cards blocked and have been reported to football association KNVB for a nationwide stadium ban.

The bans follow several weeks of investigation, including video footage analysis. They include the people who set off the fireworks and those who are accused of coordinating the attacks. Many reportedly held up banners or hid beneath them to avoid the cameras.

“It cannot be ruled out that criminal proceedings will follow in due course,” the club said. Any further action on a national ban would then be decided by the KNVB on the basis of information from the public prosecution department.

Seven home supporters suffered burns, eye injuries and hearing damage when fireworks were fired from the away section towards the pitch and the home stands in the 12th minute of the August 23 game, which Feyenoord went on to win 5-2 after a 20-minute stoppage.

Feyenoord general manager Robert Eenhoorn described the incident as “simply terrible”. The club did not take supporters to its subsequent away games at NEC Nijmegen and PEC Zwolle, and Cambuur barred visiting fans for its home match against FC Twente before lifting the restriction.

item.title: Horse meat fraud: three arrested, seven Dutch premises raided
item.description:
Horse meat fraud: three arrested, seven Dutch premises raided

September 11, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Belgian police have arrested three suspects in an ongoing investigation into an international horse meat fraud ring, and carried out raids at 24 locations, including seven in the Netherlands.

According to the Belgian Federal Police, a horse trader in East Flanders was at the centre of a ring which faked passport and microchip information to export horses used in racing for slaughter.

European regulations stipulate that animals destined for a slaughterhouse must be fitted with a microchip that tracks, among other things, whether or not they have been treated with medication.

An investigation by Belgian authorities revealed a large number of horses exported from Ireland to mainland Europe had modified or manipulated microchips.

During the raids, more than 1,000 horses were checked and many were seized. Police also confiscated electronics and more than €100,000 in cash.

The operation was carried out with the assistance of Europol, together with Dutch, French and Irish authorities.

In 2013, the Netherlands was embroiled in a horse meat scandal after it was found in products said to be 100% beef in Britain, Sweden, Ireland and Poland. The Netherlands is a major processor of horse meat imported from abroad.

item.title: Van Weel accused of neo-colonialism in Bolle Jos extradition row
item.description:
Van Weel accused of neo-colonialism in Bolle Jos extradition row

September 11, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Sierra Leone’s chief minister has accused Dutch justice minister David van Weel of “neo-colonialism” after he appeared on a national television show to demand the extradition of fugitive drugs lord Jos “Bolle Jos” Leijdekkers.

Van Weel spoke by video link from The Hague on broadcaster AYV’s State of the Nation programme on Wednesday, saying that the Netherlands had lodged a formal extradition request more than a year ago but no progress had been made.

Leijdekkers is suspected of hiding in Sierra Leone after footage of him at a church service with the president surfaced online last year. It’s alleged he is in a relationship with the president’s daughter and has a child with her.

Major drug shipments passing through West African ports are also suspected to be orchestrated by Leijdekkers’ organisation, including the biggest cocaine shipment ever seized earlier this year, and last week a 4,000 tonne seizure in France that had sailed from Ghana.

“Show the pictures”
Sierra Leonean minister David Moinina Sengeh, the president’s most senior official, responded on the same programme, saying the pressure the Netherlands was putting on the country was “scandalous” and amounted to “neo-colonialism.”

Sierra Leone is an independent country, he said, and Van Weel should stop appearing on television and threatening to cut EU aid – adding that the country did not live on European money, Nieuwsuur reported.

“Hand on heart, our security intelligence does not know where Leijdekkers is,” Sengeh said. “We cannot go by what these guys are saying or what some people are using others to say. If they know, show the pictures.”

Sengeh also accused the Netherlands of double standards, saying Freetown had twice asked The Hague to extradite a political activist and social media commentator known as Adebayor, who lives in the Netherlands and whom Sierra Leone accuses of inciting violence during riots there in 2022.

“We sent the attorney-general there. We sent the foreign affairs minister there,” he said. “They refused extradition. Have they given us that due respect to come?”

Van Weel: “ridiculous”
Van Weel told Nieuwsuur in Dutch that the neo-colonialism accusation was “ridiculous” and that the fierce reaction showed his strategy was working. He said he had not yet received a call from Freetown indicating any acceleration of the extradition process.

The interview is the latest step in a pressure campaign that has escalated since the spring. In June, Van Weel asked the EU to halt development aid to Sierra Leone, worth €352 million for the 2021 to 2027 period, though the request has so far failed to win support from other member states. In July he travelled to Ghana to build a coalition of West African countries to lean on Freetown.

Leijdekkers has been sentenced in absentia in the Netherlands and Belgium to terms Van Weel says total around 80 years.

item.title: Cardiologists in Amsterdam and Nijmegen raided over corruption
item.description:
Cardiologists in Amsterdam and Nijmegen raided over corruption

September 11, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

National fraud investigation service FIOD has raided the homes of six cardiologists in Amsterdam and Nijmegen on suspicion of corruption, and property worth at least €1.5 million has been seized, current affairs programme Nieuwsuur reported on Friday.

The FIOD believes the doctors took money from medical supply companies, under the guise of research funding, in exchange for giving those suppliers better deals. The money may have been pocketed by the doctors and funnelled through holding companies, the FIOD said.

The raids were announced on Thursday but no details were given as to which hospitals were involved, only that they were in Noord-Holland and Gelderland. Eight addresses were searched but nobody was arrested.

Nieuwsuur and research platform Investico identified the doctors through land registry records. Two work at the OLVG hospital in Amsterdam; the other four were, until recently, at the CWZ hospital in Nijmegen.

Long-running row
The Nijmegen doctors were sacked by the CWZ last year after a dispute over money. The hospital said in May 2025 they had taken €2.7 million in “sponsorship” from medical suppliers over five years, at a time when it was buying equipment from the same companies.

The FIOD has not said whether that dispute is connected to its investigation.

Zwolle
In 2022 the FIOD raided the homes of five cardiologists at the Isala hospital in Zwolle who were suspected of taking €3.2 million from a German pacemaker maker. Waiting lists there more than doubled after two of the doctors were suspended. That case has still not come to court.

Later that year Nieuwsuur found dozens of cardiologists were taking millions from device makers without their hospitals knowing. The FIOD says tips from within the medical sector and media reports prompted the new investigation.

Neither hospital had responded to a request for comment on Friday.

item.title: All you need is a Beatles lyric, TU Delft researchers find
item.description:
All you need is a Beatles lyric, TU Delft researchers find

September 11, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Researchers at TU Delft have found Beatles lyrics and song titles in more than 3,000 titles of scientific articles, according to a new paper in the open-access journal PLOS One.

Gabriel Budel and Rob Kooij of TU Delft teamed up with Michiel Tjepkema, co-host of the Dutch Beatles podcast Fab4Cast, to look for the lyrics here, there and everywhere across the scientific disciplines.

They identified 2,237 exact references and 963 examples of creative wordplay in data from the academic database Scopus.

The most used songs were “The Long and Winding Road” (798 mentions), “With a Little Help from My Friends” (209) and “Here, There and Everywhere” (129). The most cited paper was “Attention is all you need”, the 2017 paper that introduced the architecture behind ChatGPT – and a play on “All You Need Is Love”.

According to Budel, it’s not all too much. “Some of these are genuinely brilliant. ‘The lung and winding road’ is a paper on long Covid that changes one vowel,” he said in a statement.

The undertaking was not a hard day’s night. The team used a large language model to identify the lyrics, but they couldn’t just let it be. “The three of us then went through every selected title by hand to determine if it really was a Beatles pun,” Budel said.

The group didn’t stop until they got enough. They also found lyrics from Michael Jackson and Elvis Presley, though far fewer than the Beatles.

The researchers weren’t all shook up by their findings. Pop culture references can help reach a wider audience and improve readability, they said.

item.title: Five dead and forty injured in Dutch bus crash in Switzerland
item.description:
Five dead and forty injured in Dutch bus crash in Switzerland

September 11, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Five people have died and forty injured after a serious accident involving a Dutch tour bus travelling through Switzerland.

The vehicle had 48 passengers and one driver on board when it crashed between the villages of Susch and Zernez in eastern Switzerland on Thursday afternoon, broadcaster NOS reported.

Swiss police confirmed earlier this morning that several people died and more were injured, but had to notify the next of kin before making any public announcement. Emergency services spent the evening recovering the bodies.

Swiss president Guy Parmelin said on social media he was “deeply shocked and dismayed” by the accident. “At this painful time, my thoughts are with the victims and their loved ones. I offer my sincere condolences to the families of those who lost their lives,” he said.

Dutch travel company Oad organised the trip, and the bus is owned by Hartemink, a coach firm from Eibergen in Gelderland. The group was on a tour of Austria and had taken a day trip to Switzerland. Swiss authorities have said they believe most, if not all, of the passengers are Dutch.

The cause of the accident is also not known. Swiss police told local media that no other vehicles were involved and that the crash happened at a stretch of roadworks where the lanes had been narrowed. The bus went through the crash barrier and overturned.

Local police have opened an emergency number for anyone who may have family on board: +41 81 256 56 56.
